newsitem.title: USA: Talk show killer capable of intent - psychologist.
newsitem.headline: Talk show killer capable of intent - psychologist.

text.p: Jonathan Schmitz was capable of forming the intent to murder the day he killed a fellow talk show guest even though he suffered from manic depression, a psychologist testified on Thursday.

Dr. Carol Holden, a psychologist for the Michigan State Centre for Forensic Psychiatry, said under cross-examination in Schmitz' murder trial that she did not disagree with an overall diagnosis that Schmitz suffered from mental illness.
But Holden said Schmitz did not appear to be suffering from mood or thought disorders on March 9, 1995, the day he has admitted killing Scott Amedure with two shotgun blasts.
"He told me he was capable of forming a number of intents," she said.
Three days earlier Amedure, 32, revealed he had a secret crush on Schmitz, 26, during a taping of the "Jenny Jones" talk show.

Schmitz, who says he is not gay, claims the humiliation of the show, compounded by previously diagnosed mental illness and suicidal tendencies, drove him to kill Amedure after Amedure left a suggestive note at his apartment.

Holden was a rebuttal witness called by the prosecution. But under questioning from defence attorney James Burdick, she admitted that Schmitz scored highly on a personality test measuring levels of anxiety, paranoia, and schizophrenia.

She also acknowledged that a county jail psychiatrist had to arrange for Schmitz to be transferred to a psychiatric hospital because he refused to take his anti-depressant medication, believing that others were tampering with it.
Closing arguments were scheduled to begin on Thursday afternoon and the Oakland County Circuit Court jury could begin deliberations by the end of the day.
If found guilty of first-degree murder, Schmitz faces a sentence of life in prison without parole.
